items.text: I agree with Misti Y-- that one can really love Cirque's shows and dislike *Le Rêve*. To me, the theater and visual design are the real strengths. The scenery and décor are breathtaking from start to finish, and the whole concept of the show is genuinely appealing. But that's just not a show that translates very well to live. The storyline isn't super interesting. I was there once and the stage kept mal-functioning throughout the show. It's very hard to be interested and engaged for the most part of the show. It does not work for me. I feel like the show is kind of going for that Cirque spectacle and flair that one associates with Cirque, but it really doesn't quite get there. So I'd only consider going for the chance of just experiencing that beautiful theater and show. But otherwise I think you're best off spending your money on a different show.

I spent 38 dollars on this used mechanical keyboard. I'd say I got about 38 dollars worth, maybe more.

The space bar rattles. I'll admit it's annoying every time I type, like a tray of cutlery being nudged. My hands are used to it now though. The "E" key repeats every now and then, so "meeting" becomes "meeeting". Doesn't happen often, maybe once every few paragraphs. Rare enough to forget about but frequent enough to make me re-read things before I hit send.

I tried to message the seller for some info like what switches does it use. I got sick of waiting, and just bought it anyway. Got the answer a week later, by which time it was already on my desk. Brown switches, for the record.

The comfort is why I'm keeping it. There's a bump part way down each key, so I can feel that the key's been pressed, without slamming to the bottom. I can just write some emails that are really long, and my wrist is fine after. I could never do it on a laptop.

I did think about returning it. The shipping back would have eaten a chunk out of what I paid, and I'd be typing on the laptop. So it stays, rattle and all.

Went to see this circus-y thing here in Vegas recently. Great show and I’d recommend it but I’m knocking off one star. The story was hard to follow, and some of the music picks seemed slow or not suited for the action. But the performers are incredible. They look incredible, they move very well and are incredibly athletic. But especially the women who were in the water, submerged underwater for minutes at a time. The stage and theatre are circular, so every seat gave you a good view. They use three different main entrances to the stage and that was very important during big changes in the story. Beautiful stage, setting, lighting and the whole atmosphere is really unforgettable. And prices aren’t too expensive in comparison to the big shows like O and Love. I’d like more spectacular effects like fire and things like that, but it’s not a big flaw. Overall entertaining, visually dramatic show despite problems with story and music. Definitely recommend it.

It's easy to buy the hype. We can say remote work is the saviour of work, but two years of mentoring junior developers taught me it can be really damaging for new hires. They need to sit in on design conversations, they need to see others debug issues, they need to ask questions before they've been going in circles for hours. The kind of interaction that happens organically in an office. It takes real skill to know when to cut in, when to set up a call, how to explain a problem you don't fully understand yet. That skill comes before you get a chance to learn it.

I've seen feedback issues with remote work. Comments on code reviews can feel like a final word instead of a learning opportunity. Less momentum. The juniors I mentored would improve faster if they had in person pairing, whiteboard sessions, easy access to seniors, etc.

I am not trying to push for offices or anti-flexibility. Remote work can be great for self-driven devs. But for juniors, proximity is a real booster. It gives confidence, context, and instincts. Just sending a junior off with a laptop and a calendar can be a drag on their development. It may result in less good technical leadership in the future.

At 3:17 AM, the mixer hummed, that low steady drone vibrating through the soles of Elias's boots. The air was full of suspended flour dust, all in the harsh light like snow. He wiped his hands on his apron, it had stiff fabric from dried dough and sweat. He went to the front to check the lock, more out of paranoia than necessity. And there it sat, every Thursday for six weeks. No library stamp, and the bakery isn't a branch of the municipal system. The History of Salt, the blue hardback with a spine cracked near the hinge, right there on the glass counter next to the unsold cinnamon rolls. He picked it up, cold to the touch. Opened it, expecting maybe blank pages. Then a square of paper folded in lined notebook slipped out on the counter. He unfolded it. And the handwriting was jagged. You knead with your left hand dominant. Stop favoring the right. It ruins the tension. And it was pressed hard into the fiber. He stared at the words, and the mixer ticked over to the next cycle. Looked at his own hands, red-knuckled, dusted white. He closed it. And placed it back on the glass, aligned the spine perfectly with the edge. Turned off the overhead light on the display, leaving the book in shadow.

In my experience, Apple gets a shout here. My school used to only allow Apple laptops for middle and high school students. But these cost like twice the price of PCs. The computers used to breakdown about once every month. I never dropped my laptop in the four years I used it, but the hard drive had to be replaced 5 times and the OS reinstalled countless times. A mate had a MacBook Pro that caught fire while he was watching a movie, it tripped the smoke alarm. To make it worse, Apple support didn't diagnose our issues. They just backed up our computer, wiped it, and restored our files.

My gripe also involves iPhones. I had one of the first generation iPhone, which was buggy as hell. Nowdays, Apple seem to release new iPhones every 2 months or so, and the only thing that differs between models is a slightly better camera.

I'll grant you one small point. For now, iPads are still the best tablets. But Android tablets will probably catch up.

Went to the *Awakening* show at Wynn Las Vegas. It’s okay, but it’s not one of those shows that should have anyone making a whole trip for it. I’ve been brought to Vegas my whole life, since I was a kid, and I’ve seen lots of shows before I was 21. So I’ve got a pretty accurate sense of how good these shows can be.

The circular stage is really well done. For whatever you sit at, you get an actual good view. Rare in these shows. If you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, good news, there’s a deal; tickets are normally $125 but $99 for hotel guests. This is good. There’s a few really impressive acts. Performers are strong as hell, aerialists, acrobats, things like that, but too many are the same kind of stuff that I’ve seen well-done in other Cirque du Soleil shows. The problem is the story. Not clear, or not good, or not really there at all. And too much going on. Too many visuals, too many things moving, too many things trying to be “wow.” Less would hit harder. For a few amazing feats, the show is mediocre. I wasn’t blown away. No one who went with me was blown away. A couple of my friends actually enjoyed it, so I guess if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out; it’s fine. But I wouldn’t go see it again. I wouldn’t pay $125 a second time. This is one of those shows that is like the typical, stereotypical, big Vegas show: all flashy, all huge, try to do everything, more is better. It’s not better, it’s just more messy.

Got a skateboard at Zumiez then went back to buy the rest of my gear. Initially it looked good, me, my friend, his little brother were chatting with a woman employee who was building the board. She said she was a manager. Had assembled boards every day in her whole time here and on the days she was feeling cranky and annoyed she treated the other customers badly. So the assembly took 90 minutes when I expected to take 15 or less. And she broke two screws and put them in a way that made it seem that they might be sold to another customer. She finally brought in her brother and another employee who she described as a manager to finish it or help it out. No apology. Zumiez lost my future business. Heart was smashed.

I'm a bit obsessed with keyboards so I decided to get a second hand one. This one was only $38, and it's been pretty chaotic but surprisingly good. The seller was bad on comms. I messaged them and asked the switch type before buying. Took them a week to answer, with one word. I already gambled and ordered. On the board itself, it is well loved. The spacebar rattles very annoyingly, like a loose lego brick. And the letter E repeats on me. Very funny when I type "theee" instead of "the". But somehow I love this keyboard, and its tactile feedback is excellent. Very comfortable on long agonising work emails. I did consider returning it, but what is the point of shipping back a large heavy slab of plastic for 38$. So I kept it and have become fond of its flaws. If you don't mind some DIY work and a double typing letter now and then, it's a winner for the budget.

Turkish Airlines really messed me over. My Harbin to Beijing flight got delayed and I missed the connection. But I didn't know I missed it until I got to the airport, and the person at their booth just said it is what it is, no rebooking. I had to sleep there for 24 hours or something. The next day they said all flights are overbooked and it could take days. And then said if I could pay for business. And I needed to get to Istanbul, so I was forced to. I'm so angry, and in total disbelief.

A float valve handles the trough filling by using a float attached to a valve, it goes up and down depending on the level. When the trough is low the float goes down and the valve opens and water flows in. As water rises the float rises. When the level is reached the valve closes and stops filling. Two usual causes of overflow are mineral build up or debris on the valve causing it not to close fully and misadjusted float. If you have the float too high then the valve only closes when the trough is already overflow.

We debated our all-Enron party scheduled for Dec 8. We all felt different. Many felt it would be a good chance for us to celebrate, gather and celebrate, others felt it wasn't appropriate right now. So a siphon moves water past a barrier, just uses gravity and air pressure. To start it you have to fill the tube with water so there is a continuous column. Then gravity pulls the water down in the longer leg towards the lower container. That moving down makes a partial vacuum, a low pressure spot over the top of the siphon. Then the air pressure pushing down on the source water is enough to force more water up the shorter leg, replacing that low-pressure area, keeping the flow moving. The outlet has to be lower than the source water level. The weight difference in the water columns in the two legs is what drives this. If the outlet is at the same level or even higher than the source, gravity pull isn't strong enough. You need to lower the water in the outlet leg so it is heavier than the water in the rising leg. That is where the net gravitational pull happens. Air gets in and it kills the whole process. Bubbles of air break the continuous water column, stop the suction, equalize the pressure inside the tube with the outside air. The air breaks the pull and equalizes the pressure and the water stops.

I found the sourdough during its second rise, which happened. A Thursday again. On top of the flour bin, copy of Count of Monte Cristo, Richmond Public Library stamp. I don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing. Frankly at 3:00am my brain is mostly yeast and caffeine. But tonight a piece of yellow legal paper stuck out like a bookmark. Wiped hands on my apron and there was this ghostly white smudge on the dark cloth, I pulled the note out. It said page 142, please, in this frantic spiky handwriting. "I think they're watching the drop box now." A cold draft went through the kitchen, smelled like wet asphalt and rain. Looked to the darkened front windows, only my own tired face. Didn't open the book, tucked note back in between the pages, put the book in a brown pastry bag and folded the top down twice to seal it.

Let's start with the flaws. Bought the used mechanical keyboard for $38 and honestly I think I got about $38 worth, maybe a little more. The space bar rattles, not a gentle click, but a hollow loose clatter every time my thumb hits it, kinda like a tray of cutlery being nudged. I stopped noticing it during the day but late at night it sounds louder than it has any right to. The E key also repeats occasionally, so 'meeting' becomes 'meeeting'. Happens maybe once every few paragraphs, just often enough to keep me proofreading. Communication with seller was really slow too. I asked what switches it used, didn't get a reply for a week, after the keyboard had already arrived. Brown switches for the record.

The surprising part is it's genuinely comfortable to use. The keys have a nice cushioned feel to them and I can type emails and do hours of keyboarding without it hurting my wrists. That's more than I can say for the flat laptop keyboard I was using before. Wanted to return it. Didn't feel worth the hassle. It stays on my desk, rattle, repeat keys, whatever. Quietly earning its keep. 3 stars.

Tom is the man who will drive 6 hours to bring you your passport. My name is [Name], and I am Tom's older brother. Tom is the type of brother you can count on, loyal and generous, and is always willing to drive 6 hours to save you from your own stupidity. Tom is a very reliable guy and was my bunk bed roommate until he turned 14. I was the snorer... he never was, and we fought over who got the top bunk. I have been following his life very closely for a long time. I'm very happy that he has met someone who loves him like we do, but unlike me, decided to room with him on a voluntary basis.

Ratings are 4 stars unbiased, 2.5 to me. Never really wanted to see Cirque du Soleil so this was my first show. I expected tons of backflips and extreme acrobatics, but it had way less of that, way more interpretive dancing. The performers were incredibly talented, but it wasn't really my style. But, any fan of these theatrical spectacles would probably enjoy Le Rêve. Personally, though I'd just put in $100 for those shows. Lucky I went on free tickets, I am very glad I didn't pay.

They're a resource for historians, not for me. For them it's a way of piecing together the pattern of life which is missing from official accounts. What the data shows is who came, who missed, how often and if it says why they missed school, seasonal labour, sickness, bad weather, poverty, family responsibilities, migrations, emergencies. It gives insight into the relationship between education, work, household activities and community expectations. It also shows differences in gender, age, neighborhood, social class. If we look at many years, you see shifts in school habits and public health.

The limitation is you only see what the school chose to put down. So it's very, very incomplete. They don't talk about the child's experiences. And sometimes absences are misreported, incomplete, or reflect the teachers' assumptions. So it's most useful if you're comparing to other sources.

Every Thursday at 2:17, Mara would find the library book on the bakery's back step. Always the same one, *A Field Guide to North American Moths*, with the county library sticker on the spine, pale as a ghost. There's flour worked into the cover. She returned it twice. The librarians were very polite about it. So after the third week, she just kept it next to her rye starter and said nothing.

Tonight there was rain ticking against the alley door. The ovens were breathing. She was shaping croissants. Pressing the butter into the dough. The latch did its small guilty click. She wiped her hands on her apron, opened the book, found a folded slip of paper between the Luna Moth and Promethea pages. It said: "Your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. Sorry about the crumbs."

She looked at the alley, the dented milk crates, the steam off the drains. For a second the city felt huge, then it did not. She tore a corner off the order pad and wrote, "Cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05." Put the note in the book, placed it on the warm windowsill, unlocked the back door and took the book.

The classroom activity involved comparing how different cardboard bridge models hold up. The students built some of them as simple beams, arch like, or triangular folds. The dimensions of the cardboard were same for all the models, or as close as possible. And the support was same, and the weight added gradually, and observing the behavior for bending, tipping or collapse, that's how they conducted the experiment. The problem is we are making them by hand, it is not very precise, so not enough samples to really get good conclusions. But the triangular folds are holding the weight more stably in this activity. So it shows that the geometry of the folds affects how stable they are.

She found it. The book had been just placed there. She's found the book on the steel table by the back door, under the bench where the bread peels hang. A Field Guide to Coastal Birds. The Harbor Street branch stamp inside the cover says it was due in March, yet the mail slot in that door has been nailed shut years ago. But the delivery hatch beside it, where the flour man leaves his bags, never latched properly. She checked eleven Thursdays. She asked the day staff, she checked the hatch for scratches, she even stayed once past four, with her coat on. And still, nothing. The book was always between two and four. And she was always at the ovens, back turned to the door, when it showed up. Tonight a grocery receipt from Pell's was tucked into the page on oystercatchers. The ink had gone blotchy where someone pressed too hard. It says: I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want. Marguerite thought whoever it was, they smelled of salt, because the pages did too. She pulled a pencil from her apron, and on the back of the receipt she wrote. "Bring it Thursday, I'll have a roll." She tucked the note in at the oystercatchers, put the book back on the hatch ledge, and put a warm roll in a paper bag next to it.

I live in Toronto now. I don't use Hydro Ottawa for my bills anymore, but I want to warn people about how they do the billing.
I had a Hydro Ottawa account when I rented a downtown apartment for a year. Then I moved back in with my parents to get my Masters degree. So I canceled the account officially and paid off the charges.
But then? For over a year, Hydro Ottawa kept taking payments off my personal bank account, at random, when I canceled it. I called customer service like six times, I sent them the proof that they withdrew it, etc. Customer service said, "The account was closed, nothing was happening." They never acknowledged they'd made the mistake.
My parents called them, too.
So eventually we figured out what happened. It was because we had a bill in Toronto, in Montreal, I mean, Toronto, where my parents live, where I moved back home. And they accidentally linked my banking details to my parents' account and they hadn't noticed because we were receiving refunds, refunds, refunds, so they thought that was normal. But it wasn't until I spent countless hours on the phone. Spoke to like ten different customer service reps. It was a manager who finally investigated and did look into it, and corrected it. And they only apologized and initially wouldn't refund us.
I will never, ever put my banking details anywhere. And I think what I saw is really alarming because of the recklessness of them using customer data that they shouldn't.

It was 3:40 and second batch of rye was still proofing. Marisol saw it again - library book on flour bin by back door. Its plastic jacket was cold from alley. Fourth Thursday in a row it was happening. Same book, A Field Guide to Night Birds, stamped Eastgate Branch and due three weeks ago. Every time she'd carried it to the drop box on her way home. But each Thursday it came back. Feels like the building itself had borrowed it.

Wiped hands on apron, opened it. Folded index card slid out from barn owl page: "You leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread until five. I walk my mother's dog then, because she can't anymore. I keep forgetting to return this. Maybe I keep not wanting to. —R."
She read it twice while the oven timer counted down. Outside, fan hummed, pushing warm air into dark.

Turned card over. Grease pencil she uses for marking trays. Wrote: Rye's out at 4:15. Tore a heel from yesterday's loaf, wrapped in wax paper, put book on top, and propped back door open one inch.

I used Ryan Air a lot when I was a poor student. My ex lived in Sweden so it was the cheapest way to get there. The whole experience was awful. At the airport staff confiscated my £20 L’Occitane shower gel claiming it was over liquid limit, which it wasn’t, and told me to get my money back from pharmacy, which would be buying 100ml. So did, came back, they had no idea what I was talking about. £20 gone, I was absolutely furious. Then at the gate they charged me another £5 because I had water bottle in hand luggage. It was bought inside airport too, but they still charged me. Ryan Air stopped flying LPL-Skavsta so I fly Norwegian instead. Norwegian’s customer service is bad too, ironically. At least the planes are newer and less old compared to Ryan Air.

You're not alone on this. I got a serious rain on Tuesday, and by Thursday half my Brandywines had split. Can see the seam right down the side of the fruit. It's like a dry spell followed by a deluge, old story. Inside of the fruit soaks up water faster than the skin can stretch to keep up. The Sungolds are holding out mostly, but I have a few that look like they might follow suit. You really can't avoid weather if it's already happened. Two-day schedule I'm doing more even, that helps just a bit. But once the sky lets it all out at once it doesn't matter much. Should be a decent crop from the rest of the vines. Pick off split ones for another use. It's much more of a headache with Brandywines. Their thick skin is really a liability in a storm like this. You might have more luck with Sungolds, if you can keep them from getting so much water in one go.

On thursdays, it shows up. Not at the counter but wedged behind the flour bins by the backdoor, like it knows I wouldn't see it there. Same book every time. A Field Guide to North American Moths, Elmwood Branch, the return date stamp is faded purple from age. Never seen anyone leave it. By two I'm elbow deep in rye dough and would not notice a marching band. First few weeks I just put it on the shelf near the register. Gone by Friday morning. Thursday it was back. Fine. People are weird. But I'm a guy who talks to his sourdough so I'm not judging.
Tonight there was a note tucked in page 114. The luna moth page. It says, they live one week and don't eat at all. I keep thinking what a waste to be this beautiful. And do you ever get to see the bread before it is gone. No signature. Pencil, pressed hard. Read it twice, third time while the ovens ticked. Pulled my first loaf of the night, still crackling. Wrapped it in brown paper. And set it behind the flour bins.

I think we have the same problem. Sometimes even if temperature is very comfortable, still you feel uncomfortable because of humidity. So your body is unable to release your moisture. And also it depends on air circulation. Like if the air isn't moving then you get these bad smells and CO2 from breathing. And then it lingers around you. So the room feels quite stifling and uncomfortable. So it's not just about temperature, it's about the air quality, about the humidity. ACs can cool air, and they can reduce humidity and circulation, but it's not always the case. But opening windows, using a fan, or just air circulation can be really helpful to make it feel like it's fresh air.

You hear this all the time, that remote work is good for everyone. It isn't. I've been mentoring 5 junior engineers for the past 2 years, and in my experience it's not ideal for them.

The problem isn't tickets, documentation, meetings, etc. It's not the technical part. The issue is you don't really know what you don't know. As a junior, you can't see the whole tree from your branch of the forest, and you want to jump into design discussions, you want to see someone else tackle a gnarly bug. You need to be able to ask questions immediately. If your questions snowball, you're going to spiral and end up with a bad design. In an office, you get all of this for free. But with remote work, you need to figure out if you can interrupt. Can you get a call. Can you actually ask a question to someone. And if you're a junior, that's a lot of things to learn. That's a tall order to expect people to figure out on their own.

I've watched this work go wrong. The person who wrote the code is on PTO, and you have to wait days to get an answer to a review. Or you get a short comment on a review that reads like a final judgement. It's all about the lag of communication. I have watched people grow much faster with remote. But if I'm mentoring someone junior, in person they will grow much faster. They can sit with senior, pair, talk through design on whiteboards. If you're just going to hand them a laptop and a calendar with no guidance, they won't really grow. I think it's fine for more self-directed people. For juniors, you need to learn confidence, context, judgement. If we continue doing remote and they can't really get answers to questions quickly, I think we're going to produce weaker technical leaders down the road.

Most gauges are super simple. There's an opening of known area that catches rain, and it reports depth in mm or inches. That depth is what would sit on flat ground if none drained away or soaked in. Often it uses a funnel, like a big opening that feeds into a small, narrow tube. So you're getting more precision and accuracy because a small amount of rain will be higher in that narrow tube. The scale will be marked to factor in the area ratio. The one big problem you have, especially with gauges, is wind. If you've got strong gusts, and this happens quite often, it carries raindrops past the opening, meaning you're losing count. Also, if it evaporates or splashes when you're reading it, you're getting distorted results.

Picked up this keyboard used for $38 and when it arrived I thought, that's a fair deal. A bit of dust had settled between the keys, and a few shiny spots on the caps, nothing worse than I'd expect from a second hand board.

The good stuff: its just comfortable, and I type long emails for work, and feel less cramped than I did with my flat office board. The switches have a steady feel, not too heavy. And the case doesn't slide around on my desk.

Problems though. The space bar rattles every time I hit it, loud enough I notice it on a quiet morning. One key the e, repeats sometimes, and I end up with words like 'neeed' if I type too fast. Doesn't happen constantly, but enough that I proofread more carefully.

Asked seller what switches, didn't get an answer for a full week, well after keyboard arrived. Not great.

But at $38, and the keyboard arrived with no other problem, I kept it. Sending it back was more trouble than it was worth.

So, neighborhood repair cafe, so if you want to bring stuff and have it fixed, bring it, one item per person, leave it there, and they'll fix it. So when you come in, you'll have to sign in and take a number. And hold on to the number, until you get your stuff back. So they're gonna call numbers in order. So be nearby, because they may need you or a quick decision. Not everything can be fixed, it may need parts, or they can't fix it. So make sure you get your stuff before the volunteers leave at 4:30. Once they leave, anything that isn't picked up, they're not gonna store it.

Went on a Friday at 4:30ish. No line at all. Two people about 130. It was actually more expensive than I thought it would be. I went in expecting a price like a Steakhouse. But this was more than I planned to spend. Disappointed that I couldn't eat a steak. Because it's that price. So I expected steak. There was lamb, prime rib, chicken. All stuff I feel that you can get at other Vegas buffets for way less. Seafood station, we got Alaska crab legs and rock crab claws. And we hadn't seen rock crab claws anywhere else. So it was interesting. But no crab cracker. The staff said you can get wood mallets, but we were right up against the next table and I didn't wanna smash crab shells and send the pieces flying over to them. So we just ate the legs. Older school attendance records do offer historians a lot. They're useful for piecing together how life used to be in old communities. These ledgers keep track of who was present and who wasn't. You'll see patterns there. Bad weather, disease, a bad flu outbreak, times when kids were needed in harvests. A lot of the kids weren't in school because somebody needed their labour for farming activities. Also, when you get a lot of no-shows by certain demographic groups, it can highlight cultural or social attitudes towards schooling. However, these records can lie. People fudged attendance records to pass funding checks and to avoid the scrutiny of the department of education. The records do not always tell the truth. And a lot of times, they don't tell you why people weren't there. The log is a record of quantity of who was present, or not present. It's not a qualitative record. So, these logs aren't really complete, but can give you the quantitative basis of how communities operate and their social structures.

You hook the float up to a pressurized water line. This means a plastic ball or block that floats, hooked up to a lever arm. When the level drops, so the cattle drink from it, this lowers the float, tilting that arm. Pulls the plunger or washer away from the seat. Water flows in. As it rises, the float rises. The arm pushes the plunger back against the seat, narrowing the opening. Stops the flow at the set level. Overflow is usually from a worn or dirty washer that can't seal. Or a float that's been punctured and waterlogged. No longer rises up enough to close the valve.
